results.result: The authors used genetically targeted calcium imaging to record VTA dopaminergic and LC noradrenergic axon activity in dorsal CA1 of the hippocampus. They expressed axon-GCaMP6s/7b in NET-Cre mice (LC neurons) and DAT-Cre mice (VTA neurons), recording 87 LC axon ROIs from 16 mice and 9 VTA axon ROIs from 8 mice during navigation in virtual reality environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C52 describe the experimental methodology with appropriate genetic tools, sample sizes, and anatomical localization. The use of Cre-driver lines with citations (C46-C47), specific sample sizes (C48-C49), and anatomical verification (C50-C52) provide adequate methodological detail for this imaging study.

results.result: In familiar rewarded environments, VTA dopaminergic axons show position-dependent ramping activity that peaks at reward locations. 88.9% of VTA axons (8/9) exhibited significant positive correlation between position and activity, with activity increasing as mice approached the reward at the end of the track.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C37, C53, C55, and C79 consistently demonstrate VTA axon ramping-to-reward behavior with quantitative support (88.9% of axons) and reference to figures. The finding is replicated across multiple analytical approaches (position binning, individual ROI analysis) and is consistent with prior work (C53 cites Krishnan et al., 2022).

results.result: LC axons in familiar environments show minimal position encoding but strong pre-movement signals and velocity correlations. Only 28.7% of LC axons showed positive position correlation while 42.5% showed negative correlation. In contrast, 72.4% of LC axons showed velocity correlation, and the majority (56/87) showed ramping activity prior to motion onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C7, C38-C39, C54, C56-C57, C70, C78, and C80 provide converging quantitative evidence for LC encoding of kinematic variables rather than spatial position. The percentages are specific and internally consistent across different behavioral measures (position, velocity, motion onset), with appropriate statistical support referenced in figures.

results.result: Both VTA and LC axons show velocity-related activity, but with different prevalence. While 72.4% of LC axons (63/87) showed significant velocity correlation, only 28.6% of VTA axons (2/9) showed this relationship, indicating heterogeneity in VTA axon encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C62, C65-C67 demonstrate velocity encoding in both populations with clear quantitative differences. The small VTA sample size (n=9) is acknowledged, and the heterogeneity interpretation (C67) is appropriately cautious and supported by citation to similar findings in VTA soma recordings.

results.result: Reward removal experiments demonstrate that VTA ramping activity is driven by reward expectation rather than sensory cues or movement. When reward was removed, VTA position-related ramping significantly decreased while LC activity remained unchanged, and VTA pre-movement activity disappeared while LC pre-movement activity persisted.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61, C68-C69, C74-C75, C106-C108 describe a well-controlled manipulation (reward removal) that dissociates reward-related from other behavioral signals. The differential effects on VTA vs LC axons (C58 vs C59, C74 vs C75) provide strong evidence for distinct functional roles. The interpretation is supported by prior work (C108 cites Krishnan et al., 2022).

results.result: Upon exposure to a novel environment, LC axons showed dramatic sustained increases in activity (elevated for >90 seconds across 6 laps), while VTA ramping-to-reward dynamics disappeared. 36 LC axon ROIs from 10/16 mice showed significant novelty responses, while VTA axons showed reduced activity in the novel environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C42-C43, C82-C85, C88, C90-C93, and C124 provide converging evidence for divergent novelty responses. The LC response is quantified with specific time courses (90s, 6 laps) and prevalence (36/87 ROIs from 10/16 mice). The VTA lack of novelty response is documented (C85, C42) though limited by small sample size (acknowledged in C87).

results.result: One VTA axon showed increased activity following novelty exposure, suggesting potential heterogeneity in VTA responses. The authors acknowledge that the small VTA sample size (n=9) may not be representative of the full population and that their findings contrast with some prior studies showing VTA novelty responses in cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 and C111-C112 appropriately acknowledge limitations. The single responsive VTA axon (C86) is insufficient to establish a novelty response, and the authors correctly note this may reflect sampling limitations (C87, C112). The contrast with prior literature (C111) is noted but the discrepancy could arise from methodological differences (axons vs soma, experimental paradigm) rather than representing a true biological difference.

results.result: The novelty-induced LC activity has two components: a pure novelty signal lasting ~40 seconds (2 laps during running, 30 seconds during immobility) and a behavior-induced component lasting ~90 seconds (6 laps) driven by increased time spent running. Lap-by-lap analysis shows that behavioral correlations (position, velocity, motion onset) are disrupted in the first lap but recover by the third lap.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C102 describe a sophisticated dissection of novelty vs behavioral contributions to LC activity. The two-component model (C97) is supported by separate analyses of running vs immobile periods (C95-C96) and lap-by-lap recovery of behavioral correlations (C98-C101). The interpretation is logical and well-supported by the data, though the mechanistic basis remains speculative.

results.result: LC axons showed elevated activity for 20 seconds following abrupt exposure to a familiar environment from darkness, suggesting general responsiveness to unpredicted environmental changes beyond novelty per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 describe an additional control experiment (n=50 ROIs from 9 mice) showing LC responses to familiar environment onset. The shorter duration (20s vs 90s for novel) supports the interpretation (C104) that LC responds to abrupt changes with magnitude scaled to novelty level. This strengthens the arousal interpretation discussed later.

results.result: The authors conclude that VTA inputs encode reward information and maintain reward-location associations, while LC inputs encode novelty and kinematic information, likely reflecting arousal levels during navigation. These distinct signals contribute to differential modulation of hippocampal activity during behavior and learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C141-C143, and C147-C148 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. The reward encoding by VTA (C10, C147) and novelty/kinematic encoding by LC (C11, C148) are well-supported by the data. The arousal interpretation (C142-C143) is reasonable given that velocity, motion onset, and novelty all relate to arousal, though this remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: Velocity encoding in VTA axons persists in unrewarded and novel environments, indicating this is not secondary to reward-related activity. The heterogeneity across individual VTA axons is consistent with heterogeneous encoding in VTA dopamine cell bodies reported in prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 and C67 demonstrate that velocity encoding in VTA is independent of reward context and reflects genuine heterogeneity. The persistence across conditions (C109) rules out confounding by reward signals, and the comparison to soma recordings (C110, C67 citing Engelhard et al., 2019) provides appropriate context.

results.result: The introduction establishes that neuromodulatory inputs from VTA and LC to the hippocampus play important roles in synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, and place cell function, with VTA providing dopamine and LC traditionally thought to provide norepinephrine, though recent work suggests overlapping functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C12-C18 provide appropriate background context supported by citations. These establish the scientific rationale for the study by noting the importance of catecholaminergic modulation (C1, C12-C15) and the traditional view of separate VTA/LC functions (C17-C18) that recent work has challenged (C3).

results.result: Prior literature shows that VTA dopaminergic inputs enhance reward-location associations, modulate synaptic plasticity, and influence place field properties, while LC inputs also modulate synaptic strength, memory retention, and place field stability, with overlapping but potentially distinct roles in spatial learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C34 comprehensively review prior work on VTA and LC functions in hippocampus, all supported by appropriate citations. This establishes that while both systems affect similar processes (synaptic plasticity, place fields, memory), their specific roles may differ (C30), providing rationale for the current study's comparative approach.

results.result: Recent findings indicate considerable heterogeneity in the activity of both VTA and LC neurons, highlighting the need for projection-specific recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 establish the motivation for axon-level recordings rather than soma recordings, supported by multiple citations. This heterogeneity justifies the technical approach and explains why projection-specific measurements are necessary to understand hippocampal modulation.

results.result: The authors speculate that LC inputs during navigation may promote place cell excitability and plasticity, allowing flexible adaptation to environmental changes, based on prior work showing catecholamine effects on excitability and synaptic plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 are speculative interpretations (C119 explicitly uses 'may promote') about functional consequences. While grounded in cited prior work on excitability (C115) and plasticity (C118), these remain hypotheses requiring direct testing of LC effects on place cells, which was not performed in this study.

results.result: The authors propose that novelty-induced LC activity could enhance hippocampal function through multiple mechanisms including increased neuron activity, enhanced synaptic efficacy, place cell stabilization, and memory persistence, based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 cite prior work on novelty effects, while C125-C128 are speculative ('could increase/enhance') about mechanisms. These are reasonable hypotheses based on literature but remain untested in the current study. The speculation is appropriately cautious but would require functional manipulations to validate.

results.result: While LC inputs have been shown to affect activity levels, reward location representation, and memory linking, they have not been shown to affect contextual memory formation or place map stabilization in dorsal CA1. The authors speculate that novelty-induced LC activity might impact instant place field formation in novel environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 accurately cite prior work on what LC does and does not affect. Claims C134-C135 are speculative ('it is possible', 'suggesting') about instant place fields. The temporal correlation (LC signal peaks when instant fields form, C135) is suggestive but correlational; causal testing would be needed.

results.result: The authors propose a speculative mechanism whereby high LC activity during novelty might lead to dopamine release (before conversion to norepinephrine), while low LC activity during familiar exploration allows norepinephrine release, potentially explaining dopaminergic effects of LC inputs reported in prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 cite prior work on dopaminergic mechanisms and norepinephrine increases. Claims C139-C140 present a speculative hypothesis ('it is possible') about activity-dependent neurotransmitter switching. This is an interesting mechanistic proposal but remains entirely speculative without direct measurements of neurotransmitter release or conversion kinetics.

results.result: The authors propose that LC inputs may encode arousal levels that impact hippocampal neuron function, drawing parallels to LC effects on cortical tuning properties and known effects of attention/engagement on place cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 appropriately cite prior work on LC-arousal relationships in cortex and attention effects on place cells. Claim C146 is speculative ('could impact') about the mechanism in hippocampus. While the arousal interpretation is reasonable given the behavioral correlates, direct measurements of arousal or causal manipulations would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The study used only male mice due to technical limitations with headplate attachment on smaller female skulls. Mice were housed in reverse light/dark cycles and experiments were conducted during the dark phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 describe methodological details. The sex limitation (C149) is transparently reported with justification, though this represents a limitation for generalizability. Housing and testing conditions (C150-C151) are standard practices for circadian alignment.

results.result: The current findings are consistent with prior reports that LC inputs encode velocity, VTA neurons show ramping to reward, LC shows pre-movement activity, and LC cell bodies respond to novelty.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C71, C89, C105, C113-C114 appropriately contextualize findings within prior literature through citations. These comparisons strengthen the validity of the results by showing consistency with independent studies using different methods (soma vs axon recordings, different brain regions).

results.result: VTA dopaminergic axons in dorsal CA1 exhibit ramping activity that increases along the track and peaks at the reward location. This ramping activity is present in the vast majority (88.9%, 8/9) of VTA axons and reflects the animal's proximity to an expected reward rather than sensory experience.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with one stating 'VTA, but not LC, axons showed marked reward position-related activity, showing a ramping-up of activity when mice approached a learned reward position.' The editor notes 'the observed divergence in the dynamics of activity in the dopaminergic and noradrenergic axons is solid.' The data analysis is described as 'thorough' and 'rigorously analysed.'

results.result: LC axons display pre-movement signals that ramp up during the 2 seconds leading to motion onset, with the majority (56/87) of LC ROIs showing increased activity predictive of the animal's transition from immobility to movement.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. One reviewer states 'activity of LC axons ramped up before initiation of movement' and another notes 'LC-CA1 axons are activated by walking onset.' The finding is described as 'consistent with recordings of LC axons by others in dCA1 and in the cortex.'

results.result: Both VTA and LC axons show velocity-correlated activity, but with different proportions: 72.4% of LC axons (63/87) versus only 28.6% of VTA axons (2/9) showed significant positive relationships with velocity. LC velocity encoding is condition-invariant, persisting in unrewarded environments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding, stating 'activity of both VTA axons and LC axons increased with the mice's running speed' and 'LC input activity remained constant across the track, but correlated invariantly with velocity.' One reviewer notes the analysis is 'thorough and possible confounding variables and data interpretation are carefully considered.'

results.result: Following exposure to a novel environment, LC axons showed dramatic increases in activity that remained elevated for over 1 minute (approximately 90 seconds or 6 laps), with 36 LC axon ROIs from 15/22 sessions showing significant increases above baseline.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding, with one stating 'LC axons showed a dramatic increase in activity lasting 90s (6 laps) following the environment switch.' The editor notes 'the data are rigorously analysed' and the finding is described as providing 'solid evidence.' Reviewers acknowledge the revised manuscript included 'additional evidence of increased (but transient) signal in LC axons.'

results.result: Following exposure to a novel environment, VTA axon ramping-to-reward dynamics disappeared, with periodic activity in the mean of VTA axons vanishing. However, one VTA ROI showed increased activity, indicating heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant concern about this finding due to severe underpowering. One reviewer states 'the DA axonal recordings are severely underpowered, with recordings taken from a mere 7 axons' and notes 'The surprising lack of novelty-induced DA axon activity may be a false negative. Indeed, at least 1 axon (axon 2) appears to be showing novelty-induced rise in activity.' The authors acknowledge 'the lack of a novelty signal on average may be due to a small sample size.'

results.result: Reward removal experiments confirmed that VTA ramping activity is driven by proximity to expected reward: the slope of VTA population activity across positions significantly decreased when reward was removed, while LC population activity remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding, with one stating 'A subset of recordings taken when the reward was removed showed diminished ramping activity in VTA DA axons, but no changes in the LC axons, confirming that DA axon activity is locked to reward availability.' The experimental design is acknowledged as controlling for sensory experience.

results.result: Analysis separating running and immobility periods revealed two components of LC activity during novelty: a shorter purely novelty-induced increase (first 2 laps/40s during running, 30s during immobility) and a longer behavior-induced increase (6 laps/90s total).
results.evaluation: Reviewers initially requested this analysis and subsequently accepted the findings. One reviewer notes 'The revised manuscript included additional evidence of increased (but transient) signal in LC axons after a transition to a novel environment during periods of immobility.' After revisions, the reviewer states 'The authors have addressed my concerns in a thorough manner.'

results.result: LC axons showed elevated activity for 20 seconds following transition from darkness to a familiar environment, suggesting LC axons may be generally responsive to abrupt and unpredicted environmental changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as supporting evidence. One reviewer notes this shows 'that LC input to dCA1 may not solely signal novelty' and asks 'Is the overall claim that LC input to the dHC signals novelty still valid based on observed findings?' This indicates the reviewer accepts the data but questions the interpretation scope.

results.result: The study recorded 87 LC axon ROIs from 22 imaging sites in 16 mice and 9 VTA axon ROIs from 8 imaging sites in 8 mice, with all VTA axons in Stratum Oriens and LC recordings distributed across Stratum Oriens (78 axons) and Stratum Pyramidalis (9 axons).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise significant concerns about sample size, particularly for VTA recordings. One reviewer states 'the DA axonal recordings are severely underpowered, with recordings taken from a mere 7 axons (compare to 87 LC axons)' and notes 'Changes in activity in 4/7 axons are also referred to as a 'majority' occurrence in the manuscript, which again is not an accurate representation.' Another reviewer notes 'to improve reproducibility, it would be preferable to have predefined target sample sizes.'

results.result: The study used NET-Cre mice with axon-GCaMP6s to record LC noradrenergic neurons and DAT-Cre mice with axon-GCaMP7b to record VTA dopaminergic neurons.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raises methodological concerns, stating '2 different calcium indicators with differential kinetics and sensitivity to calcium changes (GCaMP6S and GCaMP7b) were used (n=3, n=4 respectively) and the data pooled. This makes it very challenging to draw any valid conclusions from the data.' This suggests the use of different indicators may confound comparisons between VTA and LC recordings.

results.result: VTA and LC inputs encode distinct information: VTA inputs encode reward information and distance to reward, while LC inputs encode novelty, kinematic information (velocity and motion onset), and likely reflect arousal levels during spatial navigation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the functional dissociation, with one stating 'the authors provide convincing evidence that activity of VTA and LC axons projecting to dorsal CA1 reflect partly distinct environmental, behavioral and cognitive factors.' The editor notes this provides 'important findings on the differential activity' and the study 'provide[s] a functional dissociation between these catecholamine projections to CA1.'

results.result: The strong velocity-correlated activity in a small subset of VTA DA axons indicates heterogeneity in the activity of these inputs, consistent with heterogeneous encoding in VTA DA cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation without challenge. The finding is presented as consistent with previous literature on VTA heterogeneity, and reviewers note the 'methodological rigor' of the analysis approaches.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support VTA axon ramping-to-reward behavior. OpenEval cites 88.9% quantitative support across multiple analyses (C4-C6, C37, C53, C55, C79), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the finding as 'solid' with 'thorough' and 'rigorous' analysis. High agreement on this core finding.

Both support LC encoding of kinematic variables rather than spatial position. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence for velocity and motion onset encoding (C5, C7, C38-C39, C54, C56-C57, C70, C78, C80), while peer reviewers accept LC axons 'ramped up before initiation of movement' and 'correlated invariantly with velocity.' Strong concordance.

Both support velocity encoding in VTA and LC populations. OpenEval notes quantitative differences and acknowledges small VTA sample size (C40-C41, C62, C65-C67), while peer reviewers affirm 'activity of both VTA axons and LC axons increased with the mice's running speed' with 'thorough' analysis. Agreement on finding despite sample size concerns.

Both support LC novelty response with sustained activity. OpenEval documents 90s/6 lap duration and prevalence (36/87 ROIs, C8-C9, C42-C43, C82-C85, C88, C90-C93, C124), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'dramatic increase in activity lasting 90s' as 'solid evidence' with 'rigorous' analysis. Strong agreement.

Both express uncertainty about VTA novelty response due to severe underpowering. OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN noting single responsive axon insufficient (C86-C87, C111-C112), while peer reviewers raise 'significant concern' about 'severely underpowered' recordings from 'mere 7 axons' and note potential false negative. Strong concordance on limitation.

Both support reward removal experiment dissociating reward from behavioral signals. OpenEval emphasizes differential VTA vs LC effects (C58-C61, C68-C69, C74-C75, C106-C108), while peer reviewers confirm 'diminished ramping activity in VTA DA axons, but no changes in the LC axons' as validating reward-locked activity. Strong agreement.

Both support two-component model of LC novelty response. OpenEval describes sophisticated dissection with running vs immobile analyses (C94-C102), while peer reviewers initially requested this analysis and subsequently accepted findings showing 'increased (but transient) signal in LC axons...during periods of immobility.' Agreement after revision.

Both support LC response to familiar environment onset as additional control. OpenEval notes shorter duration (20s vs 90s) supports arousal interpretation (C103-C104), while peer reviewers accept data but question whether 'LC input to dHC signals novelty still valid' given this finding. Agreement on data, mild divergence on interpretation scope.

Both strongly support main conclusions of functional dissociation. OpenEval affirms VTA reward encoding and LC novelty/kinematic encoding are well-supported (C10-C11, C141-C143, C147-C148), while peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence' of 'partly distinct environmental, behavioral and cognitive factors' as 'important findings.' Strong concordance on primary conclusions.

Both support VTA velocity encoding as genuine heterogeneity independent of reward. OpenEval notes persistence across conditions and comparison to soma recordings (C109-C110, C67), while peer reviewers accept interpretation without challenge, noting 'methodological rigor.' Agreement on heterogeneity interpretation.

Divergent evaluations of sample size adequacy. OpenEval supports methodology with 'appropriate' sample sizes and anatomical verification (C44-C52), while peer reviewers express 'significant concerns' about 'severely underpowered' VTA recordings (7 vs 87 LC axons) and note lack of predefined target sample sizes. Major disagreement on methodological rigor.

Divergent evaluations of calcium indicator methodology. OpenEval supports use of Cre-driver lines with citations as 'appropriate genetic tools' (C44-C47), while peer reviewer raises concern that pooling data from 'different calcium indicators with differential kinetics' (GCaMP6S and GCaMP7b) makes it 'very challenging to draw any valid conclusions.' Significant methodological disagreement.

OpenEval supports background/rationale claims about catecholaminergic modulation and traditional VTA/LC views (C1-C3, C12-C18) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory contextual claims.

OpenEval supports comprehensive literature review on VTA and LC functions in hippocampus (C19-C34) as well-cited and establishing rationale for comparative approach. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval supports motivation for axon-level recordings based on heterogeneity literature (C35-C36). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this methodological justification.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative interpretations about LC effects on place cell excitability and plasticity (C115-C119), noting these remain hypotheses requiring direct testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative claims.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative claims about novelty mechanisms (C120-C128), noting these are reasonable but untested hypotheses requiring functional manipulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative claims about instant place fields (C129-C135), noting temporal correlation is suggestive but requires causal testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative interpretations.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative hypothesis about activity-dependent neurotransmitter switching (C136-C137, C139-C140), noting this remains entirely speculative without direct measurements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this mechanistic proposal.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN arousal interpretation and attention effects (C144-C146), noting this is reasonable given behavioral correlates but would benefit from direct arousal measurements or causal manipulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific interpretive claims.

OpenEval supports methodological transparency regarding sex limitation with justification (C149-C151), though notes generalizability limitation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.
